title: Summer and Harbor
premise: Marine biologist Orsen Underhill has spent five years counting sea turtles and avoiding the town of Harbor, where her late grandmother's orchard sits rotting and half-remembered. When a clerical error names both Orsen and her estranged first love, Wren Calloway, as co-inheritors of the deed, the two are legally bound to restore the orchard together before the autumn festival or lose it to a developer who has been quietly buying up the coast. As they graft old trees and unearth why Wren vanished years ago, Orsen learns her grandmother engineered the shared inheritance deliberately, believing love left untended can still bear fruit. At the festival's end, with the developer's final offer on the table, Orsen chooses to let Wren stay past the last train — signing away her escape route and claiming a future she stopped believing she deserved.
about_author: Oscar Fairweather is the pen name of a former tide-pool docent who writes love stories set in fading coastal towns. They live in a drafty house above an orchard they are slowly learning to prune.

chapters.title: The Deed That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A lawyer's letter drags Orsen back to Harbor, where she discovers her grandmother's will names her and Wren Calloway — the woman who broke her heart and disappeared — as joint heirs to the orchard. Wren arrives unannounced, equally furious. The emotional beat is reluctant collision: two people bound by paper to a place neither can forgive.

chapters.title: Grafting Season
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Forced by the will's terms to work the orchard together through summer, Orsen and Wren fall into an uneasy rhythm of pruning, arguments, and accidental honesty. Orsen finds her grandmother's letters hinting at a secret about Wren's departure. The beat is thawing intimacy shadowed by an old wound neither will name.

chapters.title: What the Storm Took
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A storm flattens half the orchard days before the festival, and the developer swoops in with a buyout that would erase their debt. In the wreckage, Wren confesses she left years ago because Orsen's family threatened her, and that the grandmother knew. The climax: betrayal resurfaces, but so does the truth that staying was always the braver choice.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. On festival night, with the offer expiring at midnight and the last train leaving at eleven, Orsen must decide whether survival means selling or staying. She burns the buyout, tells Wren to miss the train, and together they replant what the storm took. The resolution is chosen vulnerability: love kept, not counted.
